title: Justice Minister Unveils Bill Stripping INDH's Power to File Criminal Complaints, Calling Institute 'Left-Wing Tinted'; Director Fires Back
detail: Justice Minister Fernando Rabat detailed on August 2, 2026 a draft law ('anteproyecto'), developed under the Undersecretariat of Human Rights following 2025 budget-law indications, that would restructure the National Human Rights Institute (INDH) on two fronts: its governing composition and its powers. Rabat argued 'hoy la sociedad civil está mal representada en el INDH y tiene absolutamente un tinte de izquierda, y eso hay que corregirlo' (today civil society is poorly represented in the INDH and it has an absolutely left-wing tint, and that has to be corrected), and said the government wants to eliminate the institute's power to file criminal complaints ('deducir querellas criminales'), which he called an 'anomaly,' pushing INDH toward a purely consultive role aligned with the UN Paris Principles; he aims to send the bill to Congress within weeks. On August 5, INDH director Yerko Ljubetic confronted Rabat directly before the Chamber's Human Rights Commission, rejecting the 'abuse of querellas' framing: 'de más de 6.000 querellas presentadas por el instituto... solo tenemos siete casos de condenas en costas' (of more than 6,000 lawsuits filed by the institute, we only have seven cases of cost-condemnations). Government-coalition legislators largely backed Rabat — RN deputy Ximena Ossandón proposed merging the executive bill with an existing parliamentary motion — while opposition lawmakers and the INDH defended the institute's autonomy, calling the move the most concrete step yet toward Kast's original 2021 campaign pledge to shut the institute down outright.

media.caption: INDH director Yerko Ljubetic confronts Justice Minister Fernando Rabat over the government's reform bill

title: IACHR Holds First-Ever Hearing on Alleged Human Rights Rollbacks Under Kast, Presses Government for Search-Plan and Budget Records
detail: The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (CIDH/IACHR) held a hearing in Washington on August 5, 2026 — its first devoted specifically to human-rights policy under President Kast — requested by Londres 38, the Red de Observadoras en Justicia y Memoria, the Agrupación por la Memoria Histórica Providencia Antofagasta, and the Asociación por la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos Colonia Dignidad, and joined by the public-employees' union ANEF on labor concerns. Organizations alleged: dismantling of the Justice Ministry's Human Rights Program, the state's main prosecutor of crimes against humanity, and of the Human Rights and Indigenous Peoples Unit within the Ministry of National Assets; that only 72 of 1,132 identified former detention/torture sites hold official state recognition, with subsequent reporting adding that only 5 of 33 memory sites have secured permanent funding, leaving just 8 able to access the 2026 competitive fund; suspension of expropriation proceedings for the former Colonia Dignidad grounds; and so-called 'indultos pasivos' (passive pardons) — instructing Human Rights Program lawyers to abstain from or withdraw appeals in at least 20 of 23 hearings involving convicted human-rights violators, contributing to the release of at least two convicts, César Manríquez Bravo and Héctor Osses Yáñez. The CIDH requested the government supply antecedents on the National Search Plan for Truth and Justice, the ex-ante technical evaluations behind the institutional changes, and the budget readjustments, reminding Chile that fiscal adjustments must respect the principle of non-regression. The government's Human Rights Subsecretariat denied the allegations, describing the changes as 'administrative reorganization' and insisting on policy 'continuity.'

media.caption: The Kast government faces its first IACHR hearing over alleged human-rights and memory-policy rollbacks
